title: Reliability-first field scripts and benchmarks vs LLM APIs
body:
Purpose
A compact, field-friendly note for AEs and SEs to lead conversations when buyers care about uptime, predictable latency, and graceful degradation. This is not a generic feature list; it is a scenario playbook with scripts, a small comparative snapshot focused on reliability tradeoffs, and recommended concessions/next steps for deal progression.

Context and why this matters
- Problem: Many customers we talk to have moved past model capability questions and are focused on serving reliability, predictable tail latency, and deterministic cost when traffic spikes. Competitors emphasize model access and simplicity but often lack hardened routing, fallback paths, and isolation options.
- Our angle: Redwood is about predictable inference economics and availability at scale. Position the conversation around failure modes and predictable outcomes, not just raw throughput numbers.

Target personas
- Platform/Infra leads: care about isolation (VPC/private), SLAs, and deterministic performance under noisy neighbors.
- Product engineering managers: care about latency percentiles, release control, and feature flag rollouts for model changes.
- Head of ML/ML engineers: care about evaluation regressions, rollback paths, and reproducible model versions.

Core message pillars (short)
1) Reliability-first routing: automatic fallback to compatible model variants and regional capacity tiers when primary endpoints degrade.
2) Predictable tail latency: SLO-backed serving profiles and autoscaling policies tuned for 99.9th percentile behavior, plus KV/prefix caching to cut token work for repeat requests.
3) Cost predictability: dedicated/reserved capacity options with clear burst policies; tooling to show per-token cost breakdowns by route and token type.
4) Unified ops model: same API/rollout primitives across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, so customers can migrate without refactoring routing logic.

Quick comparative snapshot (what to emphasize in 30s)
- Competitors A/B (generic categories)
  - Simple hosted-only APIs: easy to start, minimal controls for latency SLO or isolation. No private control plane. Fallbacks are ad-hoc.
  - Managed endpoints with autoscale: can hit noisy neighbor issues and unbounded cost under bursty traffic. Models might be black-box with limited rollback primitives.
  - Self-hosted runtimes: full control but heavy ops lift; often missing a unified control plane and runbook for graceful degradation.
- Redwood differentiator summary
  - Predictable SLOs + routing policies + reserved capacity and private deployment options. Notes: emphasize 'graceful degradation' examples (regional failover, lower-cost model fallback).

Field scripts and objection handling (short scripts you can read aloud)
- Objection: 'We need the lowest latency possible, so we think a managed endpoint from X is faster.'
  - Reply: 'Totally understand. In our benchmarks the median TTFB can be similar, but where teams see surprise outages or latency tails is under contention and noisy workloads. Redwood offers SLO-backed serving profiles and dedicated pools so you get predictable 99th/99.9th percentile latency, and automated regional fallback if a pool degrades. If you want, we can run a short spike test with your representative payload to show tail behavior under your pattern.'

- Objection: 'Hosted pricing from provider Y seems cheaper for our average QPS.'
  - Reply: 'Average cost is easy to reduce by throttling or caching, but unpredictable bursts cause cost spikes. Redwood has a cost ladder: reserved capacity to lock predictable unit economics, burst policies for occasional spikes, and tooling that shows token-level cost by route. We also provide guidance on batch/quantization settings tailored to your workload so we can get you to your target cost per inference.'

- Objection: 'We need a private control plane or on-prem; public APIs are out.'
  - Reply: 'We support private deployments with the same API and rollout primitives. That means you can test on hosted, then move to a private control plane without changing your calls or CI/CD. We also integrate with KMS/HSM and provide audit logs to help with compliance requirements.'

Failure-mode demo checklist (what SEs should demo)
1) Canary rollout and automatic rollback: show a canary with lower traffic and an intentional regression, trigger the rollback rule.
2) Model fallback demo: primary model fails or slows down, show transparent routing to a compatible quantized variant and minimal user-facing impact.
3) Capacity exhaustion scenario: throttle by token and demonstrate reserved capacity + burst policies working together.
4) Latency tail chart: show 95/99/99.9 percentiles before and after prefix caching for repeated queries.

Deal negotiation and concession matrix (what we can give up, what matters)
- Short-term concessions (low friction)
  - 60-90 day free pilot of Dedicated pool for critical routes.
  - Extended retention on observability exports for pilot customers.
- Mid-term concessions (require approvals)
  - Preferential on-call engineering hours for launch week.
  - Custom autoscaling rules or policy work with solutions engineering.
- Red lines (do not concede)
  - SLA-free public endpoints without reserved capacity for unlimited traffic.
  - Deep changes to runtime scheduling that compromise multi-tenant safety.

Quick rebuttal cheatsheet (short lines)
- 'We can handle bursts ourselves' -> 'Great, we can integrate with your burst strategy; our reserved pools reduce your operational complexity and preserve predictability.'
- 'We need the absolute cheapest per-token cost' -> 'If cost is the only axis, we can point to aggressive quantization + reserved capacity combos; but many teams trade a small unit cost for predictable SLOs and lower overall failure cost.'
- 'We already use another provider' -> 'Can we map your current outage or cost spikes? If you can share a week of traces, we can simulate the same workload and show where Redwood would behave differently.'

Metrics and success signals to track in a pilot
- 99th and 99.9th percentile latency on production-like traffic (target improvement or parity)
- Variance in daily serving cost across burst days (target: reduce peak-to-average ratio)
- Number of degraded requests recovered by automated fallback in pilot window
- Time-to-rollback for model regressions during canary windows

Internal notes and experiment ideas
- Collect a set of 3 customer workloads for a 'reliability demo kit' (chat support, e-commerce recommendations, and large-batch embeddings). Standardize load profiles and expected failure injection points.
- Run side-by-side spike tests with a generic hosted endpoint from a competitor and quantify 95/99/99.9 percentiles, cost delta after burst, and % of requests served by fallback policies.
- Hook Confluence page INF-ops-reliability-comparisons to pilot artifacts and make a short public-facing one-pager tailored to platform leads.

Next actions for the field
- AE: pick 2 target accounts where reliability is a stated purchase criteria and propose a 6-week pilot.
- SE: prepare a reliability demo kit using the three standard workloads and validate canary/rollback flows.
- PM: document the minimal SLAs and guardrails we promise during pilots and get legal/finance signoff on pilot concession matrix.

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep scripts conversational, not technical laundry lists. Use customer anecdotes.
- Push for pilot data capture up front (logs, token breakdown) so we can run a convincing before/after.
- If prospect is ops-heavy, lead with private deployment and audit log examples.

End of brief
This is intentionally lean. Use it as a script and living doc. Update after 2 pilot wins with concrete numbers to replace the generic claims.
